analysis.one_liner: Ends the insurance industry's blanket exemption from federal antitrust laws.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have applied federal antitrust law to insurance pricing, never got past the Senate Judiciary Committee; it received hearings in April 1989 but no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, a federal law called the McCarran-Ferguson Act has exempted the insurance business from the antitrust laws that forbid price-fixing and collusion. This bill would repeal that blanket exemption, making price-fixing among insurers illegal under the Sherman Act, while still allowing insurers to cooperate on a short list of activities: sharing historical claims data, filing standard policy forms, rating public fire defenses, fighting fraud, and running legally supervised insurance pools for people who cannot get coverage elsewhere. It would also reaffirm that states keep regulating insurance.
analysis.who_benefits: Insurance buyers — drivers, homeowners, businesses, and anyone who pays premiums — through more competitive pricing and the legal ability to challenge collusion among insurers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill states in its findings that the industry's broad antitrust exemption 'has adversely affected free competition and consumers of insurance,' and its purpose is to promote competition and protect insurance consumers. [S3]

It makes the federal antitrust laws — the Sherman Act, Clayton Act, and FTC Act — apply to the business of insurance, ending the era in which insurers could agree among themselves on rates with little federal antitrust risk. [S3]

It bans boycotts and coercion outright and bars insurers from agreeing with each other to use any rate under workers' compensation and employers' liability rating systems, while letting states keep their uniform rating plans. [S3]

It preserves useful cooperation: sharing historical claims data (with data going to state regulators), standard policy forms, fire-defense classifications, fraud information, and state-approved residual market pools that cover people no ordinary insurer will take. [S2] [S3]
It phases in over one year and bars treble damages or criminal penalties for the first two years for conduct that was lawful before enactment, giving the industry a transition period. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Insurance companies, which would lose their exemption from price-fixing and collusion lawsuits and face federal antitrust enforcement over rating and market conduct.

drawbacks.text: The insurance industry's main argument for the McCarran-Ferguson exemption is that shared actuarial data and advisory organizations let smaller insurers stay competitive and keep coverage available in difficult markets; exposing that cooperation to antitrust suits could raise legal costs and, industry supporters argue, premiums. [S3]

The bill exempts only conduct on a specific safe-harbor list, so insurers operating near the line between permitted data-sharing and prohibited rate agreements would face costly litigation during the transition. [S3]
The two-year shield against treble damages and criminal penalties for previously lawful conduct means some anticompetitive conduct during the phase-in carries reduced consequences. [S3]
The bill leaves insurance regulation with the states, so even with antitrust exposure, rate regulation would remain a patchwork of state rules rather than a uniform federal system. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the gain is real: price-fixing among insurers would become illegal, and the safe harbors are narrow enough to cover the genuinely useful cooperation. For the industry, the cost is exposure to private treble-damages lawsuits and DOJ enforcement. The main legitimate worry is transition friction — the bill tries to handle it with a one-year delay and a two-year damages shield, though that same shield also softens accountability during the changeover.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee held hearings on it in April 1989, but never reported it out, so it never reached the Senate floor before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Howard Metzenbaum, joined by Senators Simon, Biden, and Kennedy, introduced the bill on April 6, 1989. [S3] [S5]
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced. [S5]
The Judiciary Committee held hearings on April 18, 1989, printed as S.Hrg. 101-486 — the only recorded action beyond the referral. [S5]
No further action was recorded for the rest of the 101st Congress, which ended January 3, 1991, so the bill died in committee without a floor vote. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The insurance industry kept its blanket exemption from federal antitrust law, and insurers continued to set rates free of the collusion rules that apply to most other businesses.

against.name: Insurance industry
against.role: Insurers and insurance advisory organizations protected by the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption
against.what_they_did: Long-standing, well-documented opposition to limiting the McCarran-Ferguson exemption, defending joint rate-setting and advisory-organization rating as necessary to keep coverage available.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, and its three cosponsors were all Democrats, so no roll-call record shows where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill removes the industry's blanket exemption from price-fixing and collusion lawsuits, making the Sherman Act, Clayton Act, and FTC Act apply to insurance. Insurers could no longer agree among themselves on rates with legal immunity, which is why the industry historically fought McCarran-Ferguson repeal efforts.

These insurer-controlled groups would keep safe harbors for compiling claims data and filing policy forms, but lose the protection for joint rate-setting and rating plans. The bill requires that claims data they compile be made available to state regulators.

The bill expressly reaffirms that states continue to regulate and tax insurance, requires shared claims data to flow to state agencies, and lets states keep uniform rating systems and residual market pools. Federal antitrust enforcement would be layered on top of, not replace, state regulation.
